title: Thinking Like a Debugger
summary: Debugging is a method, not a talent. This lesson sets out the method experienced engineers use: make the bug happen reliably, form a hypothesis, test it with the smallest possible experiment, and narrow the search by halving it. It covers **minimal reproductions**, **bisecting** code and history, and the habits that make the tools in the rest of this chapter effective.
markdown:
## The loop Every effective debugging session runs the same loop: ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Reproduce
make it happen on demand"] --> O["Observe
what exactly happens?"] O --> H["Hypothesise
one specific cause"] H --> T["Test
an experiment that could prove it wrong"] T -->|"wrong"| O T -->|"confirmed"| F["Fix, then check the
original reproduction"] ``` The common failure is skipping steps: changing code at random ("maybe it's this"), or fixing the first suspicious thing without confirming it caused the symptom. A fix you cannot explain is a guess, and guesses usually move a bug rather than remove it. ## Step 1: reproduce A bug you can trigger on demand is half solved. A bug that happens "sometimes" is the hardest kind, so the first job is to make it reliable: - Write down the exact steps, inputs, save file, settings and build. - Remove randomness: fix the random seed, fix the time step, record the input. - For "sometimes" bugs, run it in a loop (a script that starts the game a hundred times) and look for what the failing runs have in common. - Check the obvious variables: Debug or Release? Your machine or another? Fresh install or old settings? ## Step 2: observe precisely "It crashes" is not an observation. "It crashes with an access violation reading `0x10`, in `Inventory::weight`, called from `Hud::draw`, only after picking up an item while the inventory screen is open" is. The debugger's job (chapter 4) is to turn vague symptoms into precise ones: the exact instruction, the exact values, the exact call stack. Read error messages and crash details completely, as lesson 4.03 said for compiler errors. The address, the exception code (lesson 8.04) and the module are each clues. ## Step 3: one hypothesis at a time A good hypothesis is specific and testable: "the item pointer is stale because the inventory vector grew" can be tested with a data breakpoint or a log line. "Something's wrong with memory" cannot. Test it with the **cheapest experiment that could prove it wrong**: a conditional breakpoint, a log line, an assert, changing one input. If the experiment shows the hypothesis is wrong, that is progress too: one possibility is gone. ## Narrowing the search: halve it When you do not know where a bug is, do not read code hoping to spot it. **Bisect**: split the search space in half, find out which half contains the bug, repeat. Each step halves the remaining space, so even a huge search is short: about 10 steps for a thousand possibilities, 20 for a million. | What to bisect | How | |---|---| | **History**: which change introduced the bug? | `git bisect`: mark a known good and a known bad commit; Git checks out the midpoint, you test and answer "good" or "bad", repeat | | **Input**: which part of a level or save file triggers it? | Delete half the content; does the bug remain? | | **Code path**: where does a value go wrong? | Check the value at the midpoint of the computation with a breakpoint or log | | **Time**: when does state become corrupt? | Log or assert the invariant every frame; find the first frame it fails | The practice task implements the search at the heart of this. ## Minimal reproductions Once a bug is reliable, shrink it: remove everything that is not needed for it to happen. A 30-line program that shows the bug is far easier to reason about than a whole game, and very often the act of shrinking it reveals the cause. It is also what you need to report a bug in someone else's library or compiler. ## Habits that pay off - **Check your assumptions out loud.** Explaining the code line by line to someone else, or to a rubber duck, forces you to notice the step you were skipping. - **Change one thing at a time**, and keep notes of what you tried. - **Suspect your newest code first**, and your oldest assumptions second. - **When the impossible happens, an assumption is wrong.** "This pointer can't be null here" is a hypothesis to test, not a fact. - **After fixing, write a test** that would have caught it (chapter 17), so it stays fixed. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Changing several things at once > If the bug disappears, you do not know which change fixed it, or whether one of them just hid it. > [!warning] Debugging a different build than the one that fails > If it only fails in Release, debug the Release build (lesson 8.06). > [!warning] Stopping at the first suspicious code > Confirm it causes the symptom: does the bug go away when it is fixed, and come back when it is restored? ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What are the steps of the debugging loop? - Read the code, guess the cause, change it, ship it - Add logging everywhere, run, then fix whatever looks odd + Reproduce, observe, form one testable hypothesis, test it, repeat - Fix the most likely cause first, then try to reproduce the bug > The fix is checked against the original reproduction, which is why reproducing comes first. Then fix it and check the fix against the original reproduction. ? What is bisecting, and why is it so effective? + Halving the search space each step, so steps grow only logarithmically - Testing every commit one by one from the newest; it never misses anything - Splitting the program into two threads to see which one fails - Running the Debug and Release builds side by side to compare them > 512 commits need at most 9 tests, because each test halves what is left. ? Why make a minimal reproduction? - Because the debugger cannot load large programs - Because small programs run faster in Release builds + It is easier to reason about, and shrinking it often shows the cause > Every piece you remove without losing the bug rules something out. ? Why is reproducing a bug reliably the first step? + Without it, you cannot tell whether an experiment or fix made any difference - Because the debugger only works on reproducible bugs - It is not important; finding the code matters more > Every later step depends on being able to trigger the bug on demand. ? A bug appeared somewhere in the last 512 commits. How many tests does bisecting need, at most? - 256 + About 9 - 512 > Each test halves the range: 2⁹ = 512. ? What makes a good hypothesis? - It explains every bug in the program - It is the first idea that comes to mind + A specific cause that a quick experiment could disprove > Specific and testable is what makes progress possible. ```
ideas:
- Take a bug you fixed recently and write down, honestly, how many hypotheses you tested and whether you confirmed the cause before fixing it.
- Practise `git bisect` on a small repository: introduce a bug in one of twenty commits and find it with `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good`.
- Shrink a program that shows some compiler warning or bug down to the fewest lines that still show it.
